title: OpenMAS-GCom. A Diagnostic Benchmark for Graph-enhanced Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Kairui Yang; Xunkai Li; Kaixiang Zhang; Minghao An; Zekai Chen; Yuxuan Ba; Rong-Hua Li
sections_read: 2–4, 5, Appendix A and B intervention/record definitions
assessment: Question: attribute organizational effects beyond final scores. Design: paired edge rewiring with degrees preserved, role removal, message corruption and worker failures; shared budget limits, 29-dataset interface and 400 multi-document stress tasks. Reports configuration-specific quality and resource changes. Limits: the estimand is the complete modified execution; equal limits do not imply equal realized calls, tokens or context. Longer interactive tasks remain an extension. Gap implication: generic component diagnosis and node/edge separation are already explicit. Exact activity-controlled Web effects are not thereby settled.

title: Discovering Efficient and Explainable Communication Topologies for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems via Causal Inference
authors: Junzhi Li; Peng He; Qirui Ji; Wei Wang; Lixiang Liu; Chuxiong Sun
sections_read: Problem Formulation; E2-Explainer; Experiment; appendix token accounting and scope
assessment: Question: find task-preserving communication subgraphs. Design: mask an edge and reexecute the frozen system; combine score and semantic stability, select a budgeted executable subgraph, distill an explainer. Six reasoning/coding benchmarks with Qwen3-8B; calibration uses training inputs, transfer spans graph generators. Reports token reductions and mixed task-level accuracy changes. Explicitly distinguishes edge/node counts from realized execution cost, with stronger savings after node pruning. Limits: downstream states change naturally; generator transfer is not Web evidence-regime transfer or proof of a single edge mechanism. Gap implication: merely observing that edge sparsity fails to predict total cost is already covered.

title: PEAR: Permutation-Equivariant Adaptive Routing Multi-Agent Debate
authors: Yang Feng; Ziwei Xu; Xia Hu; Fengxiang He
publication_status: arXiv:2606.20621v2, 31 August 2026; reviewed preprint edition, venue not needed for verdict
assessment: Question: reduce positional advantage and error cascades through state-aware role assignment. Design: search relabelings of a base graph at fixed edge budget, score disagreement/confidence/influence, critique then revise. Four reasoning benchmarks and six backbones, with routing ablations and trajectory correction diagnostics. Reports gains over fixed and random routing. Limits: confidence calibration and debate cost remain concerns; equivariance theorems require exchangeability and compatible update/readout kernels. Gap implication: arbitrary seat identity, semantic roles and adaptive routing are already scientific objects. A Hotpot-only role permutation is chiefly an extension unless it establishes a new mechanism.

title: Adaptive Graph Pruning for Multi-Agent Communication
authors: Boyi Li; Zhonghan Zhao; Der-Horng Lee; Gaoang Wang
assessment: Question: jointly choose participating agents and communication strengths. Design: collect scored heterogeneous subgraphs and supervise a GNN with separate edge and node heads. Six knowledge/math/code benchmarks, gpt-4o-mini; component ablation compares pruning branches. Reports improved accuracy/cost tradeoffs. Limits: backend generality and modalities remain untested; supervision/search cost and a fixed indexed pool constrain transfer. Gap implication: participation and bandwidth are expressly separate degrees of freedom. This does not estimate the exact recipient-update-controlled effect in our scheduler.

title: AgentDropout: Dynamic Agent Elimination for Token-Efficient and High-Performance LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration
authors: Zhexuan Wang; Yutong Wang; Xuebo Liu; Liang Ding; Miao Zhang; Jie Liu; Min Zhang
assessment: Question: remove redundant participation and exchanges across rounds. Design: node dropout from trained graph weights, then edge dropout over intra/inter-round communication. Three backbones; MMLU, GSM8K, MultiArith, AQuA, SVAMP, HumanEval; prompt and completion costs, component and transfer analyses. Reports efficiency and performance gains. Limits: conventional tasks, predefined roles/prompts, and residual high token cost. Transfer tests are largely within mathematics. Gap implication: fewer active agents as an efficiency mechanism and domain transfer are established topics, though evidence-regime interventions may still add specificity.

title: What Should Agents Say? Action-state Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Chen Huang; Yuhao Wu; Wenxuan Zhang
assessment: Question: which message content helps downstream agents efficiently? Design: compare full content, concise generation, conclusions, summaries and artifacts while holding the scaffold fixed; propose Action/State/Result handoffs. Includes split-evidence HotpotQA and 2Wiki, a four-role pipeline, three Qwen3 scales, field ablations and coding-harness transfer. Reports no uniformly best naive format, and evidence-grounded handoff gains. Limits: content formats also change turns and token usage; this is not an exact-length anchoring experiment. Gap implication: broad claims that evidence handoffs outperform bare conclusions or full transcripts are already directly tested on Web QA.

title: Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
authors: Chenchen Lin; Wenhao Yuan; Xuehe Wang; Edith Cheuk Han Ngai
sections_read: Methodology; Experiments; Appendix D correlation-aware construction
assessment: Question: avoid false majorities from shared upstream evidence. Design: query-conditioned latent evidence slots, provenance priors, factor aggregation, and Expand/Trace/Stop recovery; controlled paraphrase/summary descendants plus distinct complementary entries. MemoryAgentBench, LongMemEval and LoCoMo variants; module ablations and recovery costs. Reports better arbitration and reduced correlation bias. Limits: synthetic derivations expose recorded lineage; genuine Web copying and source independence are harder to certify. Gap implication: duplicating a source versus adding independent evidence is already a direct intervention. Moving it to Wikipedia agents alone does not establish novelty.

title: When Debate Helps: Proposal Supply and Verification-Aware Readout in Multi-Agent Reasoning
authors: Zihao Zhao; Tunyu Zhang; Haizhou Shi; Yusong Zhao; Xinxi Zhang; Hao Wang
sections_read: 2–5; Appendix A intervention controls; Appendix C
assessment: Question: when does interaction recover correct minority proposals beyond voting? Design: decompose recovery/new-correctness/damage, hold proposals fixed while intervening on verification evidence, and construct coverage-selected societies. Two backbones, mathematical/scientific/multidiscipline tasks, matched computation and round-level controls. Reports headroom recovery and additional interaction effects. Limits: answer clustering, extra compute, limited open-ended validation, and damage to vote-correct cases. Gap implication: proposal supply versus selection and harmful flips are already directly studied; our E8 accounting alone is replication or application, not a new mechanism.

title: Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?
authors: Hyeong Kyu Choi; Xiaojin Zhu; Sharon Li
assessment: Question: how much debate benefit exceeds initial ensembling? Design: initial majority versus multiple debate topologies/depths, homogeneous and extended settings; stochastic belief-update analysis. Seven NLP benchmarks. Reports voting accounts for much observed benefit. Limits: the martingale conclusion relies on the modeled update assumptions; it is not a universal impossibility theorem for truth-sensitive evidence exchange. Gap implication: attribution to interaction needs a strong vote/private-compute baseline; another local vote sensitivity finding has limited novelty.

title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
authors: Hailey Joren; Jianyi Zhang; Chun-Sung Ferng; Da-Cheng Juan; Ankur Taly; Cyrus Rashtchian
assessment: Question: distinguish retrieval insufficiency from failure to use available context. Design: a query/context sufficiency definition, 115 challenging human-labeled examples to validate an autorater, stratified RAG evaluation and selective generation. FreshQA, MuSiQue-Ans and HotpotQA. Reports both unsupported answering and unused sufficient context. Limits: autorater error and context truncation; annotation is not a randomized source-access intervention. Gap implication: missing benchmark supporting sentences cannot define unanswerability, and a retrieval-versus-utilization split by itself is already established.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Conflicting Evidence
authors: Han Wang; Archiki Prasad; Elias Stengel-Eskin; Mohit Bansal
publication_status: arXiv:2504.13079v2, 12 August 2025; COLM 2025 proceedings PDF also located
assessment: Question: integrate ambiguous, noisy and misleading retrieved evidence. Design: per-document agents, iterative debate and aggregator; RAMDocs varies support imbalance and entity-swapped misinformation. FaithEval, AmbigDocs and 500 RAMDocs queries; multiple backbones and aggregator/round ablations. Reports gains and degradation as misinformation increases. Limits: constructed conflicts and substantial residual error; support multiplicity is not necessarily common-source provenance. Gap implication: document frequency, minority evidence and conflicting-source debate are existing questions, while real lineage certification remains a distinct measurement challenge.

title: Don’t Hallucinate, Abstain: Identifying LLM Knowledge Gaps via Multi-LLM Collaboration
authors: Shangbin Feng; Weijia Shi; Yike Wang; Wenxuan Ding; Vidhisha Balachandran; Yulia Tsvetkov
sections_read: PDF method sections; experiments; abstain/retrieval/multi-hop analyses; Limitations
assessment: Question: identify knowledge gaps and abstain through collaboration. Design: cooperative feedback or competing alternatives, compared with calibration/training/prompt baselines; direct QA, absolute-abstention, retrieval and multi-hop analyses. Reports improved abstention/error tradeoffs. Limits: multiple-model overhead, model contamination uncertainty, domain and knowledge/safety differences. Gap implication: collaborative abstention and selective retrieval are not new; source-conditioned utility still requires valid answerability labels rather than suppressing a vote string.

title: MoDS: Moderating a Mixture of Document Speakers to Summarize Debatable Queries in Document Collections
authors: Nishant Balepur; Alexa Siu; Nedim Lipka; Franck Dernoncourt; Tong Sun; Jordan Boyd-Graber; Puneet Mathur
assessment: Question: represent opposing document perspectives in balanced summaries. Design: moderator selects document speakers, tailors retrieval queries, builds a structured outline, and summarizes; compares content-planning and speaker-selection ablations. ConflictingQA and DebateQFS, principally GPT-4. Reports coverage/balance gains. Limits: LLM cost, prompt/model dependence and limited human evaluation; balancing perspectives is not factual independence. Gap implication: routing to document-specific expertise already has a meaningful Web application; our exact-answer traces do not validate this different output task.

title: Sequential Consensus for Multi-Agent LLM Debates: A Wald-SPRT compute governor with calibration-based failure detection
sections_read: III–V; VI-H; VII-C limitations and threats
assessment: Question: when is consensus informative enough to stop? Design: judge-score likelihood ratio, explicit conditional-iid assumption, Beta calibration, simulations and real MMLU/GSM8K evaluation. Reports savings on GSM8K but cap-bound increased cost on MMLU. Limits: consensus is not correctness, calibration/domain failures, dependence and judge cost. Simulation headline results must be separated from real results. Gap implication: a consensus-based stopping rule and its calibration failure are existing contributions. A new correctness guarantee would need assumptions and evidence absent from this repository.

title: Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology
authors: Yunxuan Li; Yibing Du; Jiageng Zhang; Le Hou; Peter Grabowski; Yeqing Li; Eugene Ie
assessment: Question: can sparse static communication preserve debate performance at lower cost? Design: vary undirected connectivity among fixed agents and debate rounds; evaluate reasoning, MathVista and preference labeling with token accounting. Reports competitive sparse performance and cost reductions. Limits: static graphs and task/model specificity; density is not a realized-compute-controlled causal effect. Gap implication: sparse-versus-dense performance/cost is a mature baseline question, not a sufficient new contribution.

title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
authors: John Schulman; Filip Wolski; Prafulla Dhariwal; Alec Radford; Oleg Klimov
assessment: The clipped surrogate is the minimum of unclipped and clipped ratio-weighted advantages. For positive advantage beyond the upper clipping point its policy-improvement term is flat. This mathematical definition supports the bounded current-code derivative check; fixing its local implementation is software validation rather than a new Web research question.

title: Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information
authors: Rui Ai; Yuqi Pan; David Simchi-Levi; Milind Tambe; Haifeng Xu
assessment: Question: exploit model heterogeneity and agreement information beyond raw vote counts. Design: accuracy-weighted and second-order label-free estimators under a formal information model, simulations and UltraFeedback/MMLU/ARMMAN evaluations, with robustness tests. Reports improvements over voting. Limits: candidate-label symmetry and conditional-independence assumptions support the simplest optimality result; broader dependence is separately treated. Open-ended prompt-specific weighting remains future work. Gap implication: a better vote rule or observed disagreement alone does not establish a novel collaboration mechanism; theoretical optimality cannot be transferred to our free-form dependent agents.
